text:
A pipeline lands raw tables in the warehouse. A dashboard shows revenue. Between the two sits a layer of models, and an analytics engineer owns it. Raw tables go in; clean, tested, documented models come out, usually built with dbt. The role sits between data engineering and analytics. Interviews test four things. Sequel and modeling: facts and dimensions, star schemas, the grain, and slowly changing dimensions. Then dbt itself: models, refs and sources, tests, materializations and documentation. Software practice: version control, continuous integration, layers from staging to marts, and sequel that doesn't repeat itself. And trade-offs: a view, a table or an incremental model, and cost against freshness.

AI has added to that core, not replaced it. Modeling, dbt and sequel still come first. What's new is a reader. Companies put ask-your-data assistants in front of their warehouses, and an assistant is only as reliable as the metric definitions underneath it. Those are an analytics engineer's work. So expect four more topics. Why text-to-sequel over raw tables gives confident wrong answers, and how a semantic layer prevents them. AI-ready modeling: documentation, tests and access rules written for a reader that is a language model. Evaluating an assistant against answers you've verified, including questions it should decline. And reviewing a dbt model an assistant wrote, for its grain, its incremental logic and duplicate metrics. Some coding rounds now allow an assistant, so ask the recruiter about each round. Part nine covers all four in depth.
